title: Vocabulary: ethics and citizenship
keyIdea: Bullying is hurting someone again and again, on purpose, when it is hard for them to stop it; online it is cyberbullying. A bystander sees it and does nothing, and an upstander acts in a safe way. Peer pressure is feeling pushed by friends. Consent means asking and getting a clear yes. Integrity is doing right when no one is watching. Every right comes with a responsibility. Ethical means right and fair, and a dilemma is a hard choice where every option has a downside. Digital citizenship is being safe, kind and fair online.

kid: Bullying is hurting someone again and again, on purpose. It is hard for them to make it stop. A fall-out between two friends, just once, is not bullying. An accident is not bullying. It is still worth fixing. Bullying online, on phones or games, is called cyberbullying.

A bystander sees bullying and does nothing. An upstander sees it and does something safe. You can tell a teacher or ask the child to play. You never have to fight. Telling an adult is not telling tales. It is how bullying stops.

Peer pressure is when friends push you to do something. A good reason helps you say no. Consent means you ask first and get a clear yes. A no means no. Integrity means you do the right thing even when no one sees. "Nobody will find out" is not a reason. It is just about getting caught.

A right is something every person should have, like being safe. A responsibility is something you should do, so others keep their rights too. Ethical means right and fair. A dilemma is a hard choice where every choice has a bad side. Digital citizenship means being safe, kind and fair online.
adult: This topic gives children aged 7 to 11 the words for right and wrong with other people: bullying, cyberbullying, bystander, upstander, peer pressure, consent, integrity, rights, responsibilities, ethical, dilemma and digital citizenship. Naming a situation helps a child decide what to do and ask for help.

The lab uses five short scenes. Learners set three switches to test whether a story is bullying. They move themselves to a choice in a playground. They pull a peer-pressure rope back with real reasons. They balance rights with responsibilities and fix a post before it goes online.

Common mistakes: calling every mean moment bullying, when bullying is repeated, deliberate and involves a power imbalance. Many children think a bystander is not involved, or that an upstander must confront the bully, when telling a trusted adult counts. Some treat a right as permission to do anything, or think a photo is fine to share without asking.

At home, use the words about real events, books and shows. Ask what an upstander could do here, or whether someone said yes first. Agree together what your child will do if they see bullying online: save it, block, and tell you.

familyTip: Pick a story from a book or TV show and ask: who was a bystander, who was an upstander, and was there a dilemma? Then agree one safe thing your child would do in that spot.

practice.prompt: For {n} weeks, an older girl takes Ruby's snack and laughs. Ruby cannot make her stop. What is this?
practice.hint: Is it again and again, on purpose, and hard to stop?
practice.explain: It has gone on for {n} weeks, on purpose, and Ruby cannot stop it, so it is bullying.

practice.prompt: Kai sees Leo left out and teased. Kai goes and tells a teacher. What is Kai?
practice.hint: Did Kai do something safe to help?
practice.explain: Kai acted in a safe way by telling an adult, so he is an upstander. A bystander does nothing.

practice.prompt: {n} friends tell Ella to share a photo of Mo. Mo has not said yes. What should Ella think about?
choices: Consent: Mo has not said yes
practice.hint: Which word means asking first and getting a clear yes?
practice.explain: Even with {n} friends pushing, the photo is Mo's to agree to. Without his yes, Ella should not share it.

practice.prompt: You have the right to be safe at school. Which responsibility goes with it?
choices: Not to hurt or scare others
practice.hint: Everyone else has the same right as you.
practice.explain: Others have the right to be safe too, so your responsibility is not to hurt or scare them.

practice.prompt: Which post shows good digital citizenship?
choices: A photo of a friend, after she said yes
A joke about a classmate's hair
practice.hint: Is it safe, kind and fair?
practice.explain: Asking first is fair, and the post is kind and safe. The joke is unkind, and the address is not safe.

pool.prompt: Tom and Jas fall out once over a game and both shout. Is it bullying?
choices: No, it was once, and they are equals
pool.hint: Bullying is again and again, with more power.
pool.explain: A one-off fall-out between equals is not bullying. It is still worth sorting out.

pool.prompt: For {n} days, a group sends Sami mean messages in a game chat. What is the best word?
pool.hint: Where is it happening, and is it again and again?
pool.explain: It is repeated, on purpose and online for {n} days, so it is cyberbullying.

choices: Someone who sees bullying and does nothing
pool.explain: A bystander sees it and does nothing. Doing nothing lets bullying carry on.

pool.prompt: Ava finds £{n} on the floor. Nobody saw it drop. She hands it in. What does this show?
pool.hint: Which word means doing right when no one is watching?
pool.explain: Nobody would know if she kept the £{n}, so handing it in shows integrity.

pool.prompt: Which is a responsibility, not a right?
pool.hint: A responsibility is something you should do for others.
pool.explain: Being safe and learning are rights. Not stopping others learning is the responsibility that protects their right.

pool.prompt: Lena can tell the teacher who broke the window and upset her friend, or say nothing and feel bad. What is this?
pool.hint: Every choice here has a downside.
pool.explain: A dilemma is a hard choice where every option has a downside.

pool.prompt: Before posting, Raj asks his {n} friends in the photo, and they all say yes. What did he get?
pool.hint: He asked first and got a clear yes.
pool.explain: Asking all {n} friends and getting a clear yes is consent.

pool.prompt: Which upstander action is safest when you see bullying in the playground?
choices: Laugh so they leave you alone
pool.hint: An upstander acts, and stays safe.
pool.explain: Telling a trusted adult is a safe way to act. You never have to fight, and laughing along is joining in.

visual.caption: Bystander or upstander? Ask: did they do something safe to help?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: test stories with bullying switches, choose bystander or upstander, pull back peer pressure, balance rights and fix a post.
